title: "Viewing the Mountain, Inside the Situation"
title_zh: "观山与局中"
---

{{% en %}}
When you can see the full shape of the mountain, the mountain has already moved far away from you; when you can see the whole picture of an event, you are no longer inside it.

{{% augmented %}}
*The following content is generated by LLMs and may contain inaccuracies.*

**Context**

This note makes two claims. The first is about space: by the time you can see the whole mountain clearly, the mountain is already far away from you. The second is about your situation: by the time you can see the whole of an matter, you are no longer inside it. Taken together, the two sentences say that **seeing the whole** and **being inside it** are hard to achieve at the same time. The more complete your view, the further you are from actual participation.

This question spans several fields: epistemology (can a perspective be transcended?), cognitive psychology (how does psychological distance change understanding?), philosophy of history (understanding always arrives too late), and everyday decision-making and wisdom. It shares a root with two old Chinese sayings but takes the idea further:

- Su Shi's poem *Inscribed on the Xilin Wall* reads: "Viewed from the side it is a ridge, from the front a peak; near or far, high or low, each view differs. I cannot tell the true face of Mount Lu, only because I am inside this mountain" ([Wikisource, "Inscribed on the Xilin Wall"](https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/題西林壁)). Su Shi only says that from inside the mountain you cannot see it clearly.
- The proverb "Those inside the game are confused; those watching from outside see clearly" also says only that insiders cannot see clearly.

This note goes one step further: **seeing clearly already means having left.** At this step, it is no longer just a reminder about how to conduct yourself; it states a structural trade-off.

**Key Insights**

1. **"Distance produces the whole picture" has experimental support, but the whole picture is a generalization that distance creates.** Trope and Liberman's Construal-Level Theory holds that the farther an object is from the self in time, space, social relations, or hypothetical terms, the more abstract and holistic the way a person represents it becomes. In short, from afar one sees the forest; up close, the trees ([Trope & Liberman, *Construal-Level Theory of Psychological Distance*, Psychological Review 2010](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3152826/)). The same review notes that abstraction keeps core features and drops details treated as incidental. So the "whole picture" seen from afar is not a more complete mountain but a filtered, more coherent, more prototypical one. This is an important correction to the note: seeing the whole also means losing information.

2. **The cost can be measured: distance enhances the sense of the whole but impairs judgment of detail.** Studies cited in the same review show that when psychological distance increases, people perform better on the Gestalt Completion Task (recognizing a whole from an incomplete figure). But when asked to find a missing small component in a complete figure, such as a clock face missing one hand, their performance actually gets worse ([Trope & Liberman 2010](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3152826/)). This is almost an experimental version of "viewing the mountain": the outline becomes clear, but the cracks in the rock are no longer visible. Insiders cannot see the whole situation, but they can see local textures that outsiders miss.

3. **"Inside the game, one is confused" has an empirical name: Solomon's paradox.** Grossmann and Kross conducted three experiments (N = 693) and found that people reason more wisely about others' problems than about their own: they are more willing to admit the limits of their knowledge, more attentive to compromise and change, and better at considering others' perspectives. This asymmetry disappears, however, once participants practice self-distancing (stepping back from immersion in the situation). The effect was similar in strength among younger adults (ages 20–40) and older adults (ages 60–80) ([Grossmann & Kross, *Exploring Solomon's Paradox*, Psychological Science 2014](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0956797614535400)). One point deserves attention here: in the experiments, "leaving the game" happens only psychologically; people do not physically leave. This suggests that the "already" in the note's "no longer inside it" may not be irreversible. People can step out temporarily and deliberately without waiting for events to end.

4. **On the temporal dimension, Hegel pushes this point to its extreme.** In the preface to the *Philosophy of Right*, he writes that philosophy, as thought about the world, always appears only after reality has completed its process of formation. "When philosophy paints its grey in grey, a form of life has grown old… The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk" ([Hegel, *Philosophy of Right*, Preface, 1820](https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/hegel/works/pr/preface.htm)). This corresponds precisely to the note's second sentence: seeing the whole of an event often means the event is already over, or at least that a certain form of life has already grown old. Hegel also says that philosophy "always comes too late" and cannot instruct the world on how it ought to be (ibid.).

5. **The counterview: Kierkegaard argues that observing from outside misses what matters most.** The *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (SEP) summarizes that Kierkegaard opposed "understanding reality in an abstract way, from no particular standpoint." His aesthetic figure views life with a disinterested, spectatorial attitude, as "a spectator rather than a player." Existential questions, however, arise only from the first-person perspective. Knowing abstractly that "all humans must die" is one thing; earnestly facing "what my death means for how I should live" is another ([SEP, *Søren Kierkegaard*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kierkegaard/)). The SEP also reports Johannes Climacus's view that reflection has an "inner infinitude": as long as one is still reflecting, one cannot make a decision (ibid.). From this, a sharper claim follows: seeing the whole is not only a result of stepping outside but may also be a cause of it. Once a person fully adopts the spectator's stance and sees the entire situation clearly, they often lose the capacity to act within it.

6. **Taken together: the whole and participation stand in a relation of something like complementarity.** Putting these points side by side allows the note to be restated as a more precise proposition. Insiders possess low-level, high-resolution, interest-laden knowledge; outsiders possess high-level, structural, detached knowledge. The two cannot be fully combined at the same moment from the same perspective. The practical strategy is not to choose one side but to **switch back and forth between the two distances**: act from within first, then step out temporarily through self-distancing to see the whole, and finally return to the situation carrying the structure you have seen. The author suspects that what we call wisdom may be precisely this capacity for switching, rather than standing fixed in one position. (This is an inference, not a direct conclusion of the literature cited above.)

**Open Questions**

- **Does the "whole" exist?** If what distance reveals is only abstract generalization (Construal-Level Theory), and what proximity reveals is only local detail (Su Shi), then the "true face of the mountain" may have no privileged vantage point at all. The whole may simply be one compressed representation we select at a given distance. Is the pursuit of "seeing the whole" itself therefore misleading? Might it be more worth practicing to deliberately choose which distance to use for which kind of problem?
- **Can one see the whole from within without being carried outside by it?** Hegel's owl implies that the whole can only be seen after the fact, while the experiments on Solomon's paradox show that psychological withdrawal can happen at any time. Between these two, is there a kind of "panoramic awareness from within" that preserves the first-person sense of stakes without letting those stakes block one's view? How could it be trained in organizational decision-making, entrepreneurship, or intimate relationships? And if it could be trained, would it not be precisely the kind of reflection that Kierkegaard feared would leave a person unable to act?

{{% zh %}}
当能看清山的全貌时，山已经离你很远；当你能看见一件事情的全貌时，你已经不在局中。

{{% augmented %}}
*以下内容由 LLM 生成，可能包含不准确之处。*

**Context**

这条笔记包含两个判断。第一个关于空间：等你能看清山的全貌，山已经离你很远。第二个关于处境：等你能看见一件事的全貌，你已经不在局中。两句合起来说的是：**看得全**和**身在其中**很难同时做到。看得越完整，离亲身参与就越远。

这个问题横跨几个领域：认识论（视角能不能被超越）、认知心理学（心理距离会怎样改变理解）、历史哲学（理解总是来得太晚），还有日常的决策和智慧。它和中文里的两个老说法同源，但推得更远：

- 苏轼《题西林壁》写的是“横看成岭侧成峰，远近高低各不同。不识庐山真面目，只缘身在此山中”（[维基文库，題西林壁](https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/題西林壁)）。苏轼只说身在山中看不清山。
- 俗语“当局者迷，旁观者清”也只说局中人看不清。

这条笔记多走了一步：**看清本身就意味着已经离开**。到这一步，它就不只是一句处世提醒，而是说出了一种结构性的取舍。

**Key Insights**

1. **“距离产生全貌”有实验支持，但全貌是距离造出来的概括。** Trope 与 Liberman 的解释水平理论（Construal-Level Theory）认为，对象在时间、空间、社会关系或假设性上离自我越远，人就越用抽象、整体的方式表征它，也就是远看见林、近看见树（[Trope & Liberman, *Construal-Level Theory of Psychological Distance*, Psychological Review 2010](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3152826/)）。同一篇综述还指出，抽象化的方式是保留核心特征、删掉被当作偶然的细节。所以远处看到的“全貌”并不是更完整的山，而是一种经过筛选、更连贯、更有原型感的山。这对笔记是一个重要修正：看见全貌，同时也是在丢失信息。

2. **代价能测出来：距离提升整体感，也损伤细节判断。** 同一篇综述引用的研究显示，心理距离拉大后，人在 Gestalt Completion Task（从残缺图形中认出整体）上表现更好；但在找完整图形中缺失的小部件（比如表盘少了一根指针）时，表现反而变差（[Trope & Liberman 2010](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3152826/)）。这几乎就是“观山”的实验版：轮廓清楚了，石缝看不见了。局中人看不清全局，但看得见局外人看不见的局部纹理。

3. **“局中则迷”有实证名称：Solomon's paradox。** Grossmann 与 Kross 做了三个实验（N = 693），发现人在推理别人的问题时比推理自己的问题更有智慧：更承认自己知识有限，更看重妥协和变化，也更会考虑他人视角。而只要让被试做 self-distancing（自我抽离，不再沉浸其中），这种不对称就消失了。这个效应在年轻人（20–40 岁）和老年人（60–80 岁）中程度相近（[Grossmann & Kross, *Exploring Solomon's Paradox*, Psychological Science 2014](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0956797614535400)）。这里有一点值得注意：实验里的“离开局”只发生在心理上，人在物理上并没有离开。也就是说，笔记中“已经不在局中”的“已经”或许不是不可逆的。人可以暂时、主动地出局，而不必等事情结束。

4. **时间维度上，黑格尔把这一点说到了极致。** 《法哲学原理》序言写道：哲学作为对世界的思想，总要等现实完成其形成过程之后才出现。“当哲学把它的灰色绘成灰色的时候，这一生活形态就变老了……密涅瓦的猫头鹰要等黄昏到来才起飞”（[Hegel, *Philosophy of Right*, Preface, 1820](https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/hegel/works/pr/preface.htm)）。这和笔记第二句正好对应：看见一件事的全貌，往往意味着这件事已经结束，至少是某种生活形态已经变老。黑格尔还说，哲学“总是来得太晚”，没法教世界该怎样（同上）。

5. **反方观点：克尔凯郭尔认为站在局外看会漏掉最要紧的东西。** 《斯坦福哲学百科》（SEP）总结说，克尔凯郭尔反对“以抽离的方式、从无特定视角出发理解实在”。他笔下的审美者用无利害的旁观态度看待人生，是“旁观者而非参与者”（a spectator rather than a player）。而存在性的问题只有从第一人称视角才会真正出现，比如抽象地知道“人终有一死”，和认真面对“我的死对我该怎样活意味着什么”，是两回事（[SEP, *Søren Kierkegaard*](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kierkegaard/)）。SEP 还转述了 Johannes Climacus 的观点：反思本身有一种“内在的无限性”，只要还在想，就做不了决定（同上）。由此可以推出一个更尖锐的说法：看见全貌，不只是出局的结果，也可能是出局的原因。人一旦完全以旁观姿态看清整个局，往往就失去了在局中行动的能力。

6. **综合来看：全貌和参与之间是一种类似互补的关系。** 把上面几条放在一起，笔记可以改写成一个更精确的命题。局中人掌握低层次、高分辨率、带有利害的知识；局外人掌握高层次、结构性、平静的知识。两者不能在同一时刻、同一视角里完全兼得。实际可用的策略不是选定某一边，而是**在两种距离之间来回切换**：先在局中行动，然后用自我抽离暂时出局看全貌，再带着看到的结构回到局中。笔者推测，所谓智慧可能就是这种切换的能力，而不是站在某个固定的位置上（这是推断，不是上述文献的直接结论）。

**Open Questions**

- **“全貌”存在吗？** 如果远看得到的只是抽象概括（解释水平理论），近看只能看到局部（苏轼），那“山的真面目”可能根本没有一个特权视角。所谓全貌，也许只是我们在某个距离上选定的一种压缩方式。那么，追求“看清全貌”本身是不是一种误导？更值得练习的，会不会是有意识地选择用哪种距离来看哪类问题？
- **能不能在局中看见全貌，而不被它带出局？** 黑格尔的猫头鹰意味着全貌只能事后看到，而 Solomon's paradox 的实验说明心理上的出局可以随时发生。介于两者之间，是否存在一种“局中的全景意识”：既保留第一人称的利害感，又不被利害遮住视野？它在组织决策、创业或亲密关系中能怎样训练？如果训练得出来，它会不会正好就是克尔凯郭尔担心的那种让人无法行动的反思？
